title: Magnetic-field-activated transport from band geometry in gapped nodal-line semimetals
authors: L. Medel Onofre, L. E. Sosa-Arias, A. Martín-Ruiz
abstract: We develop a nonperturbative semiclassical theory of magnetotransport in gapped nodal-line semimetals, retaining the full magnetic-field dependence of Berry-curvature and orbital-magnetic-moment corrections. Starting from a minimal two-band model, we derive exact expressions for both the intrinsic Hall response and the dissipative Fermi-surface conductivity, valid to all orders in the magnetic field within the semiclassical regime. We show that the orbital magnetic moment reconstructs the geometrically active Fermi surface, breaking the azimuthal cancellation imposed by the nodal-line geometry and thereby activating an intrinsic Hall current that is absent at zero magnetic field. The Hall response exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on the chemical potential and a strongly nonlinear magnetic-field evolution, reflecting the redistribution of geometrically active states around the nodal ring. We further demonstrate that the Fermi-surface conductivities recover the conventional Drude behavior in the weak-field limit, while acquiring quadratic and ultimately nonperturbative magnetic-field corrections together with a field-induced transport anisotropy that gives rise to a measurable planar Hall effect at intermediate fields. Both the intrinsic and dissipative responses are strongly enhanced when the Fermi level lies close to the nodal ring, where Berry curvature and orbital magnetic moment are largest. Our results identify magnetic-field-activated geometric transport as a characteristic signature of nodal-line semimetals and provide a unified framework for describing magnetotransport beyond perturbative magnetic-field expansions, together with experimentally accessible signatures of orbital-magnetic-moment physics.
summary: This paper presents a nonperturbative semiclassical theory for magnetotransport in nodal-line semimetals. It demonstrates that magnetic fields activate intrinsic Hall currents by modifying the geometrically active Fermi surface via the orbital magnetic moment. The work provides a unified framework for understanding topological magnetotransport beyond simple weak-field approximations.
main_problem: To develop a nonperturbative semiclassical theory describing magnetotransport in gapped nodal-line semimetals.
main_result: The study shows that the orbital magnetic moment reconstructs the active Fermi surface, activating an intrinsic Hall current absent at zero field, and predicts measurable planar Hall effects at intermediate magnetic fields.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Dimensionless intrinsic Hall response Σ(b, ∆, ˜µ) defined in Eq. (23). Left panel: dependence on the rescaled chemical potential ˜µ = µ/m for two values of the magnetic field, b = 0.3 (red) and b = 0.5 (blue). The response increases close to the gap edge, reaches a maximum, and then decreases as the Fermi level moves deeper into the conduction band. Right panel: magnetic-field dependence as a function of b = B/Beff for fixed values ˜µ = 1.1 (red) and ˜µ = 1.3 (blue). The linear weak-field regime is followed by a pronounced nonlinear behavior associated with orbital-magnetic-moment effects and the field-induced restriction of the phase space.

FIG. 2: Dimensionless longitudinal Fermi-surface conductivity σFS ∥, defined by Eq. (31). Left panel: dependence on the rescaled chemical potential ˜µ = µ/m for two magnetic-field strengths, b = 0.3 (red) and b = 0.5 (blue). The conductivity increases with carrier density, while the magnetic field enhances the response mainly close to the gap edge. Right panel: magnetic-field dependence for ˜µ = 1.1 (red) and ˜µ = 1.3 (blue). The weak-field behavior is followed by a pronounced nonlinear evolution resulting from the combined effects of the orbital magnetic moment and the magnetic-field-induced deformation of the Fermi surface.

FIG. 3: Dimensionless transverse Fermi-surface conductivity σFS ⊥, defined by Eq. (32). Left panel: dependence on the rescaled chemical potential ˜µ = µ/m for b = 0.3 (red) and b = 0.5 (blue). The conductivity grows monotonically with the chemical potential, while the magnetic field induces a marked anisotropic enhancement close to the gap edge. Right panel: magnetic-field dependence for ˜µ = 1.1 (red) and ˜µ = 1.3 (blue). The nonmonotonic evolution reflects the progressive competition between the field-induced deformation of the Fermi surface and the redistribution of geometrically active states contributing to transport.

FIG. 4: Dimensionless out-of-plane Fermi-surface conductivity σFS z , defined by Eq. (33). Left panel: dependence on the rescaled chemical potential ˜µ = µ/m for magnetic fields b = 0.3 (red) and b = 0.5 (blue). The conductivity increases steadily as the Fermi level moves away from the gap, with magnetic-field effects being more pronounced near the band edge. Right panel: dependence on the magnetic field for ˜µ = 1.1 (red) and ˜µ = 1.3 (blue). Deviations from the weak-field regime become evident at intermediate fields, illustrating the nonperturbative influence of the orbital magnetic moment on Fermi-surface transport.

FIG. 5: Planar Hall conductivity arising from the magnetic-field-induced anisotropy of the Fermi-surface transport. Left panel: angular dependence of the planar Hall conductivity σFS xy , given by Eq. (38), for ˜µ = 1.3 and four representative magnetic fields, b = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8. The response follows the characteristic sin(2α) dependence of Eq. (38), vanishing when the magnetic field is parallel or perpendicular to the electric field (α = 0, π/2, π) and reaching its extrema at α = π/4 and 3π/4. Right panel: maximum planar Hall conductivity, max |σFS xy | = 1
